text: Missing data remain one of the most persistent challenges in longitudinal survey research. Traditional approaches, such as listwise deletion or simple mean imputation, tend to introduce bias when the missingness mechanism is not purely random. In this paper, we propose a multiple imputation framework built on chained equations that explicitly models the joint distribution of covariates through a sequence of conditional regressions. We evaluate the approach on both simulated and real-world panel datasets, demonstrating that it substantially reduces bias in parameter estimates relative to complete-case analysis, particularly when the proportion of missing values exceeds 20%. Our results suggest that practitioners working with attrition-prone panels should favor model-based imputation over ad hoc deletion strategies whenever feasible.

Recommender systems increasingly rely on implicit feedback signals, such as clicks and dwell time, rather than explicit ratings. This shift introduces a fundamental challenge: implicit signals are inherently noisy and confound genuine interest with exposure bias. We introduce a debiasing framework that jointly estimates user preference and propensity scores using an inverse propensity weighting scheme calibrated against a small randomized logging policy. Experiments on two large-scale e-commerce datasets show consistent improvements in offline ranking metrics, with the largest gains observed for long-tail items that are systematically underexposed by the production system. We further discuss the practical trade-offs involved in deploying propensity-weighted objectives at scale, including variance inflation and the cost of maintaining a randomized exploration policy.

Understanding how neural networks generalize beyond their training distribution remains an open problem in machine learning theory. This work examines the role of implicit regularization induced by stochastic gradient descent in shaping the geometry of the loss landscape near convergence. By analyzing the spectral properties of the Hessian at local minima found by SGD versus full-batch gradient descent, we show that stochasticity consistently biases optimization toward flatter regions of the loss surface. We further connect this empirical observation to existing generalization bounds based on sharpness, providing a partial theoretical account of why overparameterized networks trained with small batch sizes often generalize better than their large-batch counterparts. Several open questions regarding the interaction between learning rate schedules and this implicit bias are discussed.

School dropout remains a pressing concern for education systems in middle-income countries, where resource constraints limit the feasibility of individualized interventions. This study develops an early-warning system based on administrative enrollment records, using a random forest classifier trained on attendance, grade repetition, and socioeconomic indicators collected during the first academic term. Applied to a cohort of over 40,000 students across a state public school network, the model achieves an area under the curve of 0.84 in predicting dropout by the end of the academic year, substantially outperforming the logistic regression baseline currently used by the education secretariat. We discuss the operational implications of deploying such a system, including the risk of reinforcing existing biases if predictions are not paired with adequately resourced interventions.

Distributed consensus protocols such as Raft and Paxos guarantee correctness under a bounded number of node failures, but their performance under adversarial network partitions has received comparatively less empirical attention. We present a systematic evaluation of leader election latency and throughput degradation across three widely deployed consensus implementations under simulated partition scenarios of varying severity and duration. Our benchmarks reveal that recovery time after partition healing is dominated not by the consensus algorithm itself but by client-side retry logic, an aspect frequently overlooked in theoretical analyses. These findings motivate a reconsideration of how distributed systems benchmarks are designed, with implications for practitioners selecting consensus libraries for latency-sensitive applications.

Regression discontinuity designs have become a cornerstone of applied causal inference, particularly in education and public policy evaluation, owing to their relatively weak identifying assumptions. However, standard implementations assume a sharp cutoff, an assumption frequently violated in administrative data where compliance with the assignment rule is imperfect. We extend the fuzzy regression discontinuity estimator to settings with heterogeneous compliance across subgroups, deriving local average treatment effect bounds under partial identification. A simulation study calibrated to a national scholarship program illustrates that ignoring compliance heterogeneity can lead to substantial bias in estimated treatment effects, particularly when compliance correlates with the running variable near the threshold.

Convolutional architectures have historically dominated medical image segmentation, but transformer-based models are increasingly competitive on benchmark datasets. In this paper, we conduct a controlled comparison between a U-Net baseline and a Swin-Transformer-based segmentation model across three distinct imaging modalities: MRI, CT, and ultrasound. Contrary to results reported on natural image benchmarks, we find that the performance advantage of transformer architectures diminishes substantially on small, domain-specific medical datasets, where the inductive biases of convolutional layers appear to compensate for limited training data. We argue that architecture selection in medical imaging pipelines should be guided by dataset scale and modality characteristics rather than by benchmark leaderboards derived from natural image tasks.

Item response theory models routinely assume local independence among test items, an assumption that can be violated when items share a common stimulus, such as a reading passage or a data table. This paper investigates the consequences of ignoring testlet effects in large-scale assessment scoring, using both simulated data and empirical data from a national mathematics examination. We show that standard unidimensional IRT models overestimate test reliability and can distort item difficulty parameters when testlet dependence is substantial, with the bias increasing as testlet size grows. A bifactor model that explicitly accounts for testlet-specific variance components is proposed as a practical remedy, and we provide guidance on when the added model complexity is empirically justified.

Software testing practices in open-source projects vary widely, yet little systematic evidence exists on how testing rigor relates to long-term project sustainability. We analyze a corpus of over 3,000 GitHub repositories, extracting metrics on test coverage, continuous integration adoption, and contributor turnover over a five-year window. Our survival analysis indicates that repositories maintaining test coverage above 60% exhibit significantly lower rates of contributor attrition, even after controlling for project popularity and initial team size. While causality cannot be firmly established from observational data of this kind, the association is robust across several alternative model specifications, suggesting that investment in testing infrastructure may have benefits for project continuity beyond code correctness alone.

Bayesian hierarchical models offer a natural framework for partial pooling of information across schools, districts, or other nested administrative units, yet their adoption in routine educational reporting remains limited. This paper presents a hierarchical model for school-level value-added estimates that shrinks noisy estimates from small schools toward the district mean, with the degree of shrinkage determined empirically from the data rather than fixed a priori. Applied to statewide standardized test data, the hierarchical estimates show markedly lower year-to-year volatility for small schools compared to unpooled estimates, while estimates for large schools remain essentially unchanged. We discuss implications for high-stakes accountability systems that currently rely on unpooled value-added scores.

Adversarial robustness and standard generalization are often treated as competing objectives in deep learning, with robust training typically incurring a measurable accuracy cost on clean data. We revisit this trade-off through the lens of feature attribution, comparing saliency maps produced by adversarially trained and standard models on a common image classification benchmark. Adversarially trained models consistently produce attributions that align more closely with human-annotated regions of interest, suggesting that robustness training induces representations that are, in some sense, more semantically grounded. We discuss whether this alignment could be leveraged as an auxiliary training signal to reduce the accuracy cost typically associated with adversarial training, and outline preliminary experiments in this direction.

The estimation of standard errors in survey data collected via complex sampling designs, including stratification and clustering, requires methods that account for the departure from simple random sampling assumptions. This paper compares three widely used variance estimation approaches, Taylor linearization, jackknife repeated replication, and balanced repeated replication, across a range of survey designs commonly encountered in national household surveys. Simulation results indicate that while all three methods perform comparably for simple statistics such as means and proportions, jackknife replication shows the most stable performance for nonlinear statistics such as quantile regression coefficients, particularly when the number of primary sampling units per stratum is small. Practical recommendations for survey statisticians selecting among these methods are provided.

Large language models fine-tuned on domain-specific corpora often exhibit catastrophic forgetting, losing previously acquired general-purpose capabilities as they specialize. This study examines the extent of this phenomenon in models fine-tuned for legal document summarization, comparing full fine-tuning against parameter-efficient approaches such as low-rank adaptation. Our results show that low-rank adaptation preserves substantially more of the base model's general language understanding, as measured by performance on unrelated benchmark tasks, while achieving comparable summarization quality to full fine-tuning on the target domain. These findings support the growing practice of using parameter-efficient fine-tuning as a default strategy when downstream deployment requires retaining broad model capabilities alongside domain specialization.

Value-added models are widely used to estimate teacher effectiveness from standardized test score gains, but their sensitivity to model specification remains a source of ongoing debate among researchers and policymakers. We compare five commonly used value-added specifications, varying in their treatment of prior achievement, student mobility, and classroom-level covariates, using six years of linked student-teacher administrative data from a large urban district. Teacher rankings derived from different specifications show only moderate correlation, with roughly 15% of teachers shifting between the top and bottom performance quintiles depending on the model chosen. These results underscore the importance of specification transparency in any accountability system that ties consequential decisions, such as compensation or dismissal, to value-added estimates.

Graph neural networks have shown strong performance on node classification tasks, but their behavior under distribution shift between training and deployment graphs is not well understood. We conduct a systematic study of performance degradation when GNNs trained on one citation network are evaluated on a structurally similar but topically distinct network, isolating the contributions of feature shift, structural shift, and label shift to the observed accuracy drop. Structural shift, particularly changes in average node degree, emerges as the dominant factor, outweighing feature-level distribution differences in most of our experiments. We propose a lightweight degree-normalization preprocessing step that partially mitigates this degradation without requiring retraining, offering a practical option for deploying pretrained GNNs in new domains.

Standardized test score distributions frequently exhibit ceiling effects near the upper end of the scale, particularly on assessments not originally designed to discriminate among high-achieving students. This paper examines the consequences of such ceiling effects for growth modeling in a statewide mathematics assessment, showing that conventional linear growth models systematically underestimate learning gains for students near the top of the score distribution. We propose a censored regression approach that explicitly accounts for the bounded nature of the scale, yielding growth estimates that are less sensitive to a student's starting position. Simulation results confirm that the bias correction is most pronounced in grades where the proportion of students scoring near the ceiling exceeds 10%.

Federated learning enables collaborative model training across decentralized data sources without requiring raw data to leave local devices, but communication overhead remains a major bottleneck in practical deployments. This work proposes a gradient compression scheme based on adaptive quantization, where the compression ratio for each client is dynamically adjusted according to local data heterogeneity, estimated via a lightweight proxy statistic computed before each communication round. Experiments across three benchmark federated datasets show that the adaptive scheme reduces total communication volume by 40% relative to fixed-rate quantization, with negligible impact on final model accuracy. We further analyze the sensitivity of the approach to the choice of heterogeneity proxy, finding that even coarse approximations yield most of the achievable communication savings.

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is commonly applied to assess distributional fit in applied statistical work, yet its asymptotic critical values are only valid when the parameters of the hypothesized distribution are known a priori rather than estimated from the same sample. This paper quantifies, through extensive Monte Carlo simulation, the degree of size distortion that results from ignoring this requirement across several common parametric families, including the gamma, Weibull, and skew-normal distributions. Size distortion is found to be most severe for distributions with three or more estimated parameters, where nominal test sizes of 5% can correspond to true rejection rates exceeding 20% under the null. A parametric bootstrap correction is demonstrated to restore approximately correct test size across all distributions considered.

Multilingual named entity recognition systems trained primarily on high-resource languages tend to transfer poorly to typologically distant low-resource languages. We investigate whether targeted data augmentation using back-translation from a related high-resource language can close this gap for a set of five low-resource languages spanning three language families. Augmentation yields consistent, though modest, improvements in entity-level F1 score, with the largest gains observed for languages sharing a common script with the source language used for back-translation. Qualitative error analysis suggests that remaining failures are concentrated on culturally specific entity types, such as local administrative divisions, that are poorly represented even in the augmented training data, pointing to a limitation of purely translation-based augmentation strategies.

Randomized controlled trials in education frequently suffer from differential attrition, where the probability of dropping out of the study correlates with the treatment assignment itself, threatening the internal validity of intention-to-treat estimates. This paper applies Lee bounds to a large-scale randomized evaluation of a computer-assisted learning intervention, comparing the resulting treatment effect bounds against the naive intention-to-treat estimate that ignores differential attrition. The bounds are found to be uncomfortably wide, spanning both statistically significant positive and null effects, despite the naive estimate suggesting a robust positive impact. We argue that differential attrition should be routinely diagnosed and reported in education RCTs, particularly for interventions delivered through channels, such as digital platforms, where dropout is easy to observe but rarely analyzed formally.

Time series forecasting under structural breaks poses a persistent challenge for classical autoregressive models, which implicitly assume parameter stability over the estimation window. We propose a rolling-window ensemble approach that combines forecasts from models estimated over multiple window lengths, weighted according to their recent out-of-sample performance, to adaptively respond to regime changes without requiring explicit break-point detection. Applied to a panel of macroeconomic indicators spanning two documented recessions, the ensemble approach reduces mean absolute forecast error by 12% relative to a single fixed-window benchmark during the twelve months immediately following each break, while showing no meaningful degradation during stable periods. The approach requires no manual tuning of break-detection thresholds, a practical advantage in automated forecasting pipelines.

Explainability methods for tabular machine learning models, such as SHAP and LIME, are increasingly used in high-stakes domains including credit scoring and clinical risk prediction, yet their stability under small perturbations of the input has received limited scrutiny. We evaluate the consistency of SHAP attributions across bootstrap resamples of a gradient-boosted tree model trained on a credit default dataset, finding that feature rankings for the top three attributed features remain stable in over 90% of resamples, while rankings for mid-tier features fluctuate substantially. This instability has direct implications for regulatory settings that require model explanations to be reproducible and defensible, suggesting that explanation stability should be reported alongside explanation accuracy in model documentation.

Peer effects in classroom settings are notoriously difficult to identify because student ability, classroom assignment, and unobserved shocks are typically correlated. This study exploits idiosyncratic year-to-year variation in the composition of incoming cohorts within schools that use non-strategic, administratively determined classroom assignment, to estimate the effect of average peer ability on individual achievement growth. We find a modest but statistically significant positive peer effect, concentrated among students in the lower half of the within-classroom ability distribution, with little detectable effect for higher-achieving students. The asymmetry in estimated effects is consistent with theoretical models in which lower-achieving students benefit disproportionately from exposure to higher-achieving peers through informal knowledge spillovers.

Quantization of large language models for edge deployment introduces a trade-off between model size, inference latency, and output quality that is not yet well characterized across model families. We benchmark four post-training quantization schemes, ranging from 8-bit to 2-bit precision, across three open-weight language models of varying parameter count, evaluating both perplexity degradation and downstream task accuracy on a standard benchmark suite. Degradation is highly nonlinear with respect to bit width, with most models retaining over 95% of full-precision task accuracy down to 4-bit quantization but showing sharp declines below that threshold. Notably, the point of sharp decline varies by nearly a full bit width across the three model families tested, indicating that quantization robustness is not a purely architectural property but depends on pretraining data and scale as well.

Spatial autocorrelation in school-level achievement data, arising from shared neighborhood characteristics and residential sorting, is frequently ignored in standard regression-based accountability models, potentially biasing standard errors and, in some specifications, point estimates as well. This paper applies a spatial error model to school-level proficiency data from a metropolitan school district, using a contiguity-based weight matrix derived from school attendance zone boundaries. Moran's I statistics confirm significant positive spatial autocorrelation in raw proficiency scores, and accounting for this structure widens confidence intervals for school-level estimates by an average of 18% relative to a naive ordinary least squares specification. We recommend that spatial dependence be explicitly tested for, and modeled where present, in any school comparison exercise conducted at the metropolitan or district level.

Chain-of-thought prompting has been shown to improve large language model performance on multi-step reasoning tasks, but the extent to which the generated reasoning steps are causally responsible for correct answers, as opposed to being post hoc rationalizations, remains contested. We design a set of counterfactual intervention experiments in which reasoning steps are systematically corrupted while the final answer format is held constant, measuring the resulting change in answer accuracy across several reasoning benchmarks. Corruption of early reasoning steps produces substantially larger accuracy drops than corruption of later steps, a pattern that would not be expected under a purely post hoc rationalization account, providing indirect evidence that chain-of-thought reasoning is at least partially causally load-bearing for the models tested.

Test equating procedures are essential for maintaining score comparability across different forms of a standardized assessment administered in different years, yet the choice of equating method can meaningfully affect the resulting score scale, particularly for assessments with limited common-item overlap between forms. This paper compares equipercentile equating and item response theory true-score equating on a state assessment with a 20% common-item anchor design, finding that the two methods produce cutscore-equivalent proficiency classifications that differ for approximately 3% of students near existing performance-level boundaries. Given the consequential nature of proficiency classifications for school accountability, we recommend that testing agencies report equating method sensitivity as part of routine technical documentation.

Vision-language models trained on web-scraped image-caption pairs inherit demographic and cultural biases present in their training data, a concern that has motivated substantial recent work on bias measurement and mitigation. We construct a targeted evaluation set probing occupational gender associations across fifty occupations, comparing association strength in a widely used open-weight vision-language model before and after a lightweight debiasing intervention based on contrastive fine-tuning on a small, curated counter-stereotypical dataset. The intervention reduces measured association strength by roughly half on the targeted occupations, but we observe a modest, statistically detectable degradation in zero-shot classification accuracy on unrelated categories, illustrating the difficulty of achieving debiasing without any cost to general model capability.

Administrative data suppression, applied by statistical agencies to protect the confidentiality of small subpopulations, introduces a form of non-ignorable missingness that is structurally distinct from typical survey nonresponse. This paper develops a maximum likelihood framework for estimating aggregate statistics from suppressed count data, explicitly modeling the suppression mechanism as a known, deterministic function of the underlying count rather than treating suppressed cells as missing at random. Applied to county-level health surveillance data subject to small-cell suppression, the proposed estimator reduces bias in estimated disease prevalence by over 30% relative to the common practice of substituting suppressed cells with a fixed sentinel value, with the improvement most pronounced in sparsely populated counties where suppression rates are highest.

Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines are commonly evaluated on end-task accuracy, but this composite metric obscures whether errors originate from the retrieval component, the generation component, or their interaction. We introduce a diagnostic evaluation protocol that decomposes end-to-end failures into retrieval failures, where no relevant document is retrieved, and generation failures, where relevant documents are retrieved but not correctly synthesized into an answer. Applying this protocol to three open-domain question answering benchmarks, we find that generation failures, rather than retrieval failures, account for the majority of errors in two of the three benchmarks, a finding that runs counter to the common assumption that retrieval quality is the primary bottleneck in these systems, and suggests that further gains may depend more on generator training than on retriever improvements.

Grade retention policies, which require students who fail to meet promotion criteria to repeat a grade, remain widely used despite mixed evidence on their long-term effects. This study uses a regression discontinuity design around an administratively determined promotion cutoff to estimate the causal effect of grade retention on subsequent test score growth and high school completion. We find that retained students show a short-term boost in test scores relative to marginally promoted peers, but this advantage fades within three years, while retained students show no significant difference in eventual high school completion rates once age-at-graduation effects are properly accounted for. The results suggest that any short-term academic benefits of retention do not translate into improved longer-run educational attainment for students near the promotion margin.

Data contamination, the inadvertent inclusion of benchmark evaluation data in large language model pretraining corpora, threatens the validity of reported benchmark performance across the field, yet standard contamination detection methods rely on exact or near-exact string matching that can miss paraphrased contamination. We propose a semantic contamination detection method based on comparing model perplexity on benchmark items against a matched set of held-out items with similar surface statistics, on the hypothesis that memorized items will show anomalously low perplexity relative to genuinely unseen items of comparable difficulty. Applied to a widely used open-weight model, the method flags a nontrivial subset of items on two popular benchmarks as likely contaminated, at rates exceeding those detected by exact-match methods, underscoring the need for more robust contamination auditing practices industry-wide.

Zero-inflated count models are frequently applied to health service utilization data, where a large proportion of individuals report no utilization in a given period alongside a right-skewed distribution of positive counts among utilizers. This paper compares the zero-inflated Poisson and zero-inflated negative binomial specifications on a national health survey dataset, using a battery of information criteria and posterior predictive checks to assess relative fit. The negative binomial variant is preferred by all information criteria considered and, critically, is the only specification that adequately reproduces the observed variance in utilization counts among the positive-count subpopulation, a distinction that has direct implications for the calibration of healthcare capacity planning models built on these estimates.

Curriculum learning, in which training examples are presented to a model in order of increasing difficulty rather than at random, has produced inconsistent results across the deep learning literature, with some studies reporting substantial gains and others finding no benefit or even harm. We conduct a controlled study isolating the effect of curriculum ordering from confounding factors such as learning rate schedule and total training compute, which are often varied jointly with curriculum strategy in prior work. Under matched compute budgets, curriculum ordering yields a small but consistent improvement on tasks with high label noise, while showing no measurable benefit on clean, well-curated datasets, suggesting that curriculum learning's apparent inconsistency in the literature may partly reflect uncontrolled variation in dataset quality across studies rather than a fundamentally unreliable technique.

Item bank calibration for computerized adaptive testing requires that item parameters remain stable across repeated administrations, an assumption termed parameter drift when violated. This paper monitors item parameter stability across five consecutive administration windows of a large-scale adaptive assessment, flagging items whose difficulty parameter shifts beyond a pre-specified tolerance using a sequential probability ratio test. Approximately 8% of items in the operational bank exhibit statistically significant drift over the monitored period, disproportionately concentrated among items covering recently revised curriculum content, a pattern consistent with instructional exposure effects rather than pure item exposure from repeated test administration. We recommend that item banks be stratified by curriculum recency when scheduling recalibration cycles.

Model compression techniques, including pruning and knowledge distillation, are typically evaluated on aggregate accuracy metrics that can mask disparate impact across subpopulations within the evaluation dataset. We audit a set of pruned image classification models across demographic subgroups defined by a secondary annotated attribute, finding that pruning-induced accuracy loss is not uniformly distributed: subgroups that were already the lowest-accuracy group in the unpruned model tend to bear a disproportionate share of the additional accuracy loss introduced by pruning. This compounding effect persists across three pruning methods and two model architectures tested, suggesting that compressed models deployed in production should undergo subgroup-level accuracy audits rather than relying solely on aggregate benchmark comparisons.

Longitudinal studies of teacher labor markets face a persistent selection problem: teachers who leave the profession or transfer schools are not missing at random with respect to the outcomes of interest, such as effectiveness or job satisfaction. This paper applies a Heckman selection correction to a panel of teacher effectiveness estimates linked to attrition records from a large state administrative dataset, comparing corrected and uncorrected trends in average teacher effectiveness over a decade. The correction reveals that reported improvements in average teacher effectiveness over the study period are substantially attenuated once selective attrition of lower-performing teachers is accounted for, indicating that a nontrivial share of apparent gains reflects compositional change in the teaching workforce rather than improvement among individual teachers who remain.

Ensemble methods that combine forecasts from multiple time series models generally outperform any single constituent model, but the optimal weighting scheme for combining forecasts remains an active area of methodological debate. We compare simple average weighting against inverse mean-squared-error weighting and a stacking approach based on a held-out validation window, across a large collection of macroeconomic and financial time series from a standard forecasting competition dataset. Simple average weighting proves surprisingly competitive with the more sophisticated alternatives across the majority of series tested, with stacking showing a meaningful advantage only for the subset of series exhibiting pronounced structural instability, suggesting that the added complexity of learned weighting schemes is not universally justified and should be reserved for series with known nonstationarity.

Automated essay scoring systems, increasingly deployed to reduce human grading costs in large-scale assessment programs, have faced persistent criticism regarding their sensitivity to superficial textual features rather than genuine writing quality. We conduct an adversarial evaluation of a widely used automated scoring engine, submitting essays deliberately padded with sophisticated but semantically empty vocabulary and syntactically complex but logically incoherent sentence structures. Padded essays receive scores on average 1.2 points higher, on a six-point scale, than matched control essays with equivalent argumentative content but simpler prose, a gap comparable in magnitude to the difference typically observed between grade levels. These findings raise concerns about construct validity when automated scores are used for consequential decisions without human review of a representative sample.

Hyperparameter sensitivity remains a practical obstacle to the reliable deployment of reinforcement learning algorithms outside of controlled benchmark environments. This study systematically varies the discount factor, learning rate, and entropy regularization coefficient across a grid of configurations for a widely used policy gradient algorithm, evaluating final policy performance and training stability on three continuous control benchmark tasks. We find that final performance is considerably more sensitive to the entropy regularization coefficient than to the other two hyperparameters across all three tasks, with narrow ranges of near-optimal values that do not transfer consistently across tasks, underscoring the practical difficulty of hyperparameter transfer even within a superficially similar family of control problems.

Cluster-robust standard errors are the default choice for inference in panel data applications with grouped error structures, yet their finite-sample performance degrades noticeably when the number of clusters is small, a scenario common in state-level or country-level panel studies. This paper compares conventional cluster-robust standard errors against the wild cluster bootstrap across a range of cluster counts, using Monte Carlo simulations calibrated to typical state-panel applications in applied economics. With fewer than 20 clusters, conventional cluster-robust inference exhibits substantial over-rejection of true null hypotheses, while the wild cluster bootstrap maintains close-to-nominal rejection rates even at 10 clusters, reinforcing existing methodological guidance that researchers working with a small number of clusters should default to bootstrap-based inference.

Synthetic control methods have become a popular tool for policy evaluation in settings with a single treated unit and a small number of potential comparison units, but their reliance on a donor pool of untreated units raises questions about robustness to donor pool composition. We conduct a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis on a published synthetic control evaluation of a state-level minimum wage increase, iteratively excluding each donor unit and re-estimating the synthetic control weights and resulting treatment effect. The estimated effect changes sign in two of the fifteen leave-one-out iterations, both involving the exclusion of a single large donor state that receives disproportionate weight in the baseline specification, illustrating that published synthetic control results can be more fragile to donor pool composition than confidence intervals based on placebo tests alone would suggest.

Speech recognition systems trained predominantly on standard dialects exhibit measurably higher error rates on regional and non-standard dialect speech, a disparity with direct implications for equitable access to voice-based technology. This paper evaluates a commercial automatic speech recognition system across five regional dialect groups within a single language, using a curated evaluation set balanced for speaker demographics and recording conditions. Word error rates vary by a factor of nearly two across dialect groups, with the disparity persisting even after controlling for background noise levels and recording equipment, indicating that the gap reflects genuine acoustic and lexical mismatch with training data rather than confounding recording conditions. We argue that dialect-stratified error reporting should become standard practice in speech recognition benchmarking.

Propensity score matching is widely used to approximate randomized experiments in observational education research, but its performance depends critically on the richness of the covariate set used to estimate the propensity score, a dependency that is difficult to verify in any single application. This paper conducts a within-study comparison, benchmarking propensity score matching estimates of a tutoring program's effect on math achievement against a gold-standard randomized controlled trial estimate of the same program. Matching on a rich administrative covariate set, including prior test scores and detailed demographic indicators, recovers an estimate within the confidence interval of the experimental benchmark, whereas matching on a sparser covariate set typical of many observational studies produces an estimate outside that interval, underscoring the sensitivity of matching-based inference to covariate selection.

Prompt injection attacks, in which adversarially crafted input text causes a language model to deviate from its intended instructions, represent an emerging security concern for applications that incorporate untrusted user or third-party content into model context. We construct a benchmark of injection attacks targeting retrieval-augmented systems, where malicious instructions are embedded within retrieved documents rather than direct user input, and evaluate the susceptibility of several widely deployed language models to this indirect injection vector. Susceptibility varies substantially across models, but no model tested achieves full robustness, and simple prompt-level defenses, such as explicit instructions to disregard embedded commands, reduce but do not eliminate successful injections, suggesting that robust defense against indirect prompt injection likely requires architectural rather than purely prompt-based solutions.

Multilevel models for cross-classified data, in which lower-level units belong simultaneously to two or more non-nested higher-level groupings, such as students nested within both schools and neighborhoods, present estimation challenges not encountered in purely hierarchical structures. This paper compares maximum likelihood and Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo estimation of cross-classified random effects models under varying degrees of cross-classification imbalance, using simulated data mimicking a student-school-neighborhood structure. Maximum likelihood estimates show appreciable downward bias in the neighborhood-level variance component when the cross-classification is highly imbalanced, a bias that the Bayesian approach avoids at the cost of substantially longer computation time, presenting applied researchers with a genuine trade-off between estimation speed and small-sample accuracy.

Data augmentation strategies for low-resource machine translation typically rely on back-translation using an auxiliary model trained on the same limited parallel data, which can propagate and amplify errors present in the auxiliary model itself. We propose an iterative refinement scheme in which back-translated synthetic data is filtered using a round-trip consistency check before being added to the training set, discarding synthetic pairs whose round-trip translation diverges substantially from the original source sentence. Across three low-resource language pairs, the filtering step improves downstream translation quality by a modest but consistent margin over unfiltered back-translation, with the largest gains observed for the language pair with the smallest original parallel corpus, where synthetic data quality has proportionally greater influence on final model performance.

Differential item functioning, where an assessment item exhibits different difficulty for examinees of equal underlying ability but different demographic group membership, threatens the fairness of standardized testing and is routinely screened for prior to test form finalization. This paper compares the Mantel-Haenszel procedure against a logistic regression-based approach for differential item functioning detection on a large-scale reading assessment, examining agreement rates and the characteristics of items flagged uniquely by each method. The two methods agree on the flagging decision for the large majority of items, but items flagged only by the logistic regression approach are disproportionately those exhibiting nonuniform differential item functioning, a pattern the Mantel-Haenszel procedure is known to have reduced power to detect, reinforcing existing recommendations that the two methods be used in combination rather than as substitutes.

Knowledge distillation compresses a large teacher model into a smaller student model by training the student to match the teacher's output distribution rather than hard labels alone, but the choice of distillation temperature, which controls the softness of the teacher's target distribution, is typically tuned empirically without strong theoretical guidance. We conduct a systematic sweep over distillation temperature across four teacher-student model pairs spanning two modalities, image classification and text classification, examining the resulting relationship between temperature and student accuracy. The temperature yielding peak student performance varies by more than a factor of three across the pairs tested, correlating most strongly with the entropy of the teacher's own predictive distribution on the training set, suggesting that practitioners could use this readily computed teacher statistic to substantially narrow the search space for temperature tuning.

Educational technology platforms increasingly generate fine-grained behavioral log data, such as time-on-task and hint-seeking behavior, that could in principle supplement or replace coarser summative assessment for formative purposes. This paper evaluates whether behavioral log features extracted from a widely used adaptive mathematics platform improve prediction of end-of-year standardized test scores beyond what is achievable using mid-year formative assessment scores alone. Log-derived features, particularly the rate of hint requests on problems of moderate difficulty, contribute a modest but statistically significant improvement in predictive accuracy, though the gain is small relative to the predictive power already captured by formative assessment scores, suggesting behavioral log data may be more valuable for real-time instructional adjustment than for summative outcome prediction.

Selection bias in administrative wage records arises because such records typically capture only formal-sector employment, systematically excluding workers in informal arrangements who may differ in unobserved ways from their formally employed counterparts. This paper develops a bounding approach for estimating the returns to a vocational training program on total earnings, informal and formal combined, using administrative formal-sector wage data supplemented with a household survey capturing informal employment status for a subsample. Under plausible monotonicity assumptions regarding the relationship between program participation and formalization, the bounds on total earnings effects are considerably narrower than worst-case nonparametric bounds, though they remain wide enough to encompass both economically meaningful positive effects and null effects, illustrating the persistent difficulty of drawing sharp causal conclusions from administrative data with structural coverage gaps.

Benchmark leaderboards for large language models have proliferated in recent years, yet the statistical significance of small performance differences between models on these leaderboards is rarely formally assessed. This paper applies paired bootstrap significance testing to head-to-head comparisons between the top ten models on a widely followed public leaderboard, finding that fewer than half of the pairwise ranking differences among these top models are statistically distinguishable at conventional significance thresholds given the benchmark's sample size. We argue that leaderboard rankings, as currently reported without uncertainty quantification, convey a misleading impression of precision, and recommend that leaderboard maintainers report confidence intervals or significance groupings alongside point-estimate rankings.

Class size reduction policies remain politically popular despite mixed causal evidence on their academic effectiveness, in part because credible identification of class size effects requires exogenous variation in class size that is difficult to obtain outside of experimental settings. This paper exploits a maximum class size rule that mechanically triggers class splitting once enrollment crosses a discrete threshold, using a regression discontinuity design around this administratively determined cutoff in a national primary school system. We find statistically significant positive effects of smaller classes on reading achievement in early grades, but the estimated effect size is roughly half that reported by the most frequently cited experimental study in this literature, suggesting that policy discussions drawing on that earlier experimental estimate may overstate the expected benefit of similarly scaled class size reduction policies implemented through administrative rules rather than randomized assignment.

Tokenization choices in large language model pretraining, particularly the size and construction of the subword vocabulary, are known to affect downstream performance, but their interaction with model scale has received limited systematic study. We pretrain a series of models spanning two orders of magnitude in parameter count under three different vocabulary sizes, holding total training compute fixed across the comparison, and evaluate downstream perplexity and task accuracy. The relative advantage of larger vocabularies increases with model scale, a pattern consistent with larger models being better able to exploit the additional embedding parameters without a proportional increase in overfitting risk, suggesting that vocabulary size should be treated as a scale-dependent hyperparameter rather than fixed independently of the target model size.

Attendance-based funding formulas, which allocate school resources partly on the basis of average daily attendance rather than enrollment alone, create a direct fiscal incentive for schools to maximize measured attendance, raising concerns about potential gaming of attendance records. This paper examines attendance reporting patterns around the specific enrollment thresholds that trigger funding formula discontinuities in a state school finance system, testing for a discontinuous jump in reported attendance rates precisely at these thresholds. We find no statistically detectable discontinuity in reported attendance at the relevant thresholds, providing some reassurance against gross manipulation, though the analysis cannot rule out more subtle forms of attendance recording behavior that would not produce a sharp discontinuity of the kind this design is powered to detect.

Contrastive pretraining objectives for sentence embeddings typically rely on large batches of in-batch negatives, but the quality of these negatives, specifically whether they are genuinely dissimilar to the anchor sentence, is rarely verified and can vary substantially depending on the source corpus. We introduce a hard-negative mining procedure that identifies semantically similar but non-paraphrase sentence pairs within the training corpus to serve as harder negatives than random in-batch sampling provides, and compare embeddings trained with and without this mining step on a standard semantic textual similarity benchmark. Hard-negative mining improves benchmark correlation by a moderate margin, with the improvement concentrated on sentence pairs exhibiting high lexical overlap but low semantic similarity, precisely the category of pairs that random negative sampling is least likely to surface during training.

Interim assessments administered several times per year are intended to provide teachers with actionable, timely information on student learning, but evidence on whether teachers actually change instructional practice in response to interim results remains limited and largely qualitative. This paper links interim assessment score reports to weekly lesson plan submissions from a sample of elementary teachers, using natural language processing to detect topical alignment between lesson content and areas of identified student weakness in the preceding interim report. Detectable alignment between lesson content and diagnosed weaknesses increases modestly in the two weeks immediately following an interim assessment cycle before reverting toward baseline, suggesting that interim data does prompt short-term instructional responsiveness, though the effect appears to fade well before the next assessment cycle begins.

Weak instrument problems in instrumental variable estimation lead to biased point estimates and unreliable standard errors, yet applied researchers frequently rely on the conventional first-stage F-statistic rule of thumb to screen for instrument strength without considering its known limitations in the presence of heteroscedasticity or clustering. This paper re-examines a set of published instrumental variable estimates from the education economics literature using the more robust effective F-statistic and associated weak-instrument-robust confidence sets recently proposed in the econometrics literature. Several instruments that pass the conventional first-stage F-statistic threshold of ten fail the more stringent effective F-statistic criterion once clustering is properly accounted for, and the corresponding weak-instrument-robust confidence intervals are, in some cases, substantially wider than the originally reported intervals, raising questions about the strength of previously published conclusions in this literature.

Active learning strategies for annotation-efficient model training typically select the most informative unlabeled examples according to a model-based uncertainty criterion, but this approach can systematically neglect regions of the input space where the current model is confidently wrong rather than uncertain. We propose a hybrid selection criterion that combines predictive uncertainty with an out-of-distribution detection score, prioritizing examples that are both uncertain and structurally dissimilar from previously labeled training data. On three text classification benchmarks with deliberately induced distributional gaps between initial labeled and unlabeled pools, the hybrid criterion outperforms pure uncertainty sampling by a margin that widens as the distributional gap increases, while the two criteria perform comparably when no such gap is present.

Cross-validation is the standard tool for model selection in applied predictive modeling, but its validity relies on an assumption of independence between folds that is frequently violated in spatial or temporal data due to autocorrelation. This paper compares standard k-fold cross-validation against spatially blocked cross-validation for selecting hyperparameters of a random forest model predicting soil contaminant concentrations from a spatially dense monitoring network. Standard cross-validation systematically selects hyperparameter configurations associated with overfitting, evidenced by substantially worse performance on a genuinely held-out spatial region, whereas spatially blocked cross-validation selects configurations that generalize considerably better to that held-out region, reinforcing methodological guidance that spatial or temporal structure in the data should dictate the cross-validation scheme used, rather than defaulting to standard random folds.
